idiom_name: function-pointer pair per representation (encode/decode table entry)
implementation_notes: C has no conversion registry and no dispatch by type, so the converter object degenerates into data: one struct per representation pair holding two function pointers (encode/decode, to_wire/from_wire, save/load) plus a tag or context pointer, selected through a table or an enum. For scalar values the standard library already supplies the pair - strtol/strtoul/strtod for text to value and snprintf for value to text - and they are inverse only if the format string is fixed and endptr and errno are checked. The struct-of-function-pointers form is the C version of the pattern and is justified as soon as more than one format or caller needs the same pair; for a single call site two static functions are enough and clearer.
pitfalls: snprintf returns the length that would have been written, so using that return value as bytes written silently truncates; compare it against the buffer size.
strtol/strtod accept trailing garbage unless endptr is verified, and out-of-range input only sets errno - checking the return value alone loses both distinctions.
Nothing in libc enforces that both directions are registered or that they are inverse; a missing direction surfaces as a NULL function pointer at runtime.
The pair carries caller-allocated buffers, so ownership and the buffer size must be part of the contract; a codec that writes past n is an overflow.
